passage: Saturday playgroup, a park in Porto. Paulo, two, pressed his lips shut when his dad held out a slice of kiwi. Green, fuzzy, strange. He pushed the hand away. On the blanket beside him, Soo-ah, three, bit into her own slice, juice dripping down her wrist. "Mmm!" she hummed, and grabbed another. Paulo watched her chew. He shuffled closer and watched again. Then he took the kiwi from his dad's palm, licked it, and bit. He held out his hand for more.

qa.q: What fruit did Paulo's dad offer him?
qa.a: His dad held out a slice of kiwi.

qa.q: What does Paulo shuffling closer and watching Soo-ah again suggest about his feelings?
qa.a: He was curious but still unsure; seeing Soo-ah enjoy the kiwi seemed to tell him it was safe to try.

qa.q: What could Paulo's dad try the next time Paulo refuses a new fruit?
qa.a: He could sit Paulo near a child who is happily eating it and let him watch, without pushing the food at him.

qa.q: How might Soo-ah feel if she noticed Paulo copying her and asking for more?
qa.a: She might feel proud and grown-up, like she had shown a younger child something good.

grounding: It shows a toddler trying a new food only after watching another child eat it happily.

passage: I'm Sudha. I was holding my little brother Tanvir on the sea wall when Papa bought roasted corn from the cart. Tanvir is two. He shoved the cob away and hid his face in my kurta. Then a small girl beside us started gnawing hers, grinning, butter on her cheeks. Tanvir peeked. He stared at her for ages. Then he grabbed the cob and bit once, eyes still on her. I can't say what changed his mind, but he finished half.

qa.q: Where was Sudha holding Tanvir when Papa bought the corn?
qa.a: Sudha was holding Tanvir on the sea wall.

qa.q: Why might Tanvir have kept his eyes on the girl while he took his first bite?
qa.a: He seemed to be checking her face for reassurance, because her happy chewing made the strange cob look safe to him.

qa.q: How could Sudha or Papa use what they saw the next time Tanvir refuses a food?
qa.a: They could let him sit with other children eating it happily instead of pushing it at him.

qa.q: How might Papa feel when he sees Tanvir finish half the corn after refusing it?
qa.a: Papa might be surprised and relieved, and a little amused that a stranger's grin worked where his offer didn't.

grounding: An older sister observes a toddler eat a new food only after seeing another child enjoy it.

passage:
Wednesday

Dear Diary,
Everybody in 5C has a squishy on their bag now. A peach one, a cloud one, a strawberry with a face. Today I counted: nineteen. NINETEEN. I asked Ammi for one after school and she asked what I like about them. I said they're squishy. She waited. I said everyone has one, so they must be good, right? Nineteen people can't all be making a mistake.
Farida doesn't have one. She says they smell like an eraser and she'd rather save for the drawing book. I squeezed Mahnoor's squishy at lunch and honestly it was just okay.
But I still want one. A cloud one.
Deepika

qa.q: How many squishies did Deepika count on bags in 5C?
qa.a: She counted nineteen.

qa.q: How does Deepika seem to feel about not having a squishy yet?
qa.a: Deepika seems left out and a little envious, since nineteen classmates have one, even though Mahnoor's squishy felt just okay.

qa.q: What question could help Deepika decide whether to spend on a squishy?
qa.a: Deepika could ask what to choose if no one in 5C had one, the way Farida thinks about the drawing book.

qa.q: How might Farida feel being one of the few in 5C without a squishy?
qa.a: She seems settled in her own choice, though she might sometimes feel left out when the others compare theirs.

grounding: A child wants the class craze because so many classmates have it, even though the child finds it only okay.

passage: The weekly haat set up beside the bus stand in Shirpur every Thursday. Nikita dragged her aunt Tanuja straight past the vegetables to the stall with the light-up pens. "This one, Maushi. The one with the blinking tip." "Do you need a new pen?" Nikita counted on her fingers. "Rupa has it, Salma has it, both Patil boys, the whole back bench. The whole of Class 6 bought it last week." "And what does it write like?" Nikita paused. "Blue." Tanuja laughed. "So many people bought it," Nikita insisted. "They must know something." Tanuja picked up a pen, clicked it, and scribbled on her palm. The ink skipped. She held it out without a word.

qa.q: Where was the weekly haat set up?
qa.a: It was set up beside the bus stand in Shirpur.

qa.q: Why did Nikita insist that the pen was good?
qa.a: She was eager to have what the whole of Class 6 had and felt confident they must know something, even though she couldn't say how it wrote.

qa.q: What turning point could help Nikita choose for herself here?
qa.a: Testing the pen on Tanuja's palm showed the ink skipping, which gives Nikita a real fact to weigh against the crowd.

qa.q: What was Tanuja hoping Nikita would notice when she held out the pen without a word?
qa.a: Tanuja seemed to want Nikita to see for herself that the pen skipped, rather than being told not to buy it.

grounding: A child wants the pen the whole class bought, trusting numbers over her own judgment of it.

passage:
Dear Gautam Bhaiya,
You asked why I sounded strange on the phone on Sunday. Here's the truth.
On Saturday night the whole group climbed the ladder on our building's water tank to take photos. Everyone went up laughing, even Shreya, who is scared of lifts. The rungs were rusty and one wobbled. My stomach kept saying no. But they all looked so relaxed, I thought maybe the problem was just me being the scaredy little sister again. So I climbed.
Halfway up my foot slipped. I scraped my palm open and hung there shaking till Neel pulled me back down.
Nobody else seemed worried at all. I keep wondering if they were just pretending too.
I told Mummy that night. She cleaned my hand, and she wasn't even angry, just quiet.
Jaya

qa.q: What happened to Jaya's foot halfway up the ladder?
qa.a: Her foot slipped, and she scraped her palm open and hung there shaking.

qa.q: What was Jaya thinking when her stomach kept saying no?
qa.a: She thought the problem might be her being the scaredy little sister, because everyone else looked so relaxed.

qa.q: At which moment could Jaya have trusted her own unease, and what might she have done?
qa.a: When she felt the wobbly rung and her stomach said no, she could have stayed on the ground and taken photos from there.

qa.q: What might Gautam Bhaiya feel on reading Jaya's letter?
qa.a: He might feel shaken that she got hurt, and glad she told Mummy and was honest with him.

grounding: A teen joins a risky climb because the group seems calm, doubting her own fear.

passage: Okay, Vinita, you want the chilli story for the show. Fine, here's Rafiq's most embarrassing night. I was sixteen, at my cousin's wedding in Hyderabad. The boys, me included, found a packet of those extreme-hot chips, the kind with the warning on the pack. One chip each, on camera. Every one of them did it, laughing, fanning their mouths, acting cool. I remember thinking: my eyes are already watering from the smell. That's a sign, right? But nobody else looked worried. So I told myself I was the problem. I ate it. Ten minutes later I was throwing up behind the tent and my Ammi was holding my head. Later my cousin Irfan admitted his stomach hurt all night too. He just didn't say. So, Vinita, that's the thing. I wasn't the only one scared. I was just the only one who thought it was only me.

qa.q: Where was Rafiq when he ate the chilli chip?
qa.a: He was at his cousin's wedding in Hyderabad.

qa.q: What did Rafiq believe about his watering eyes before he ate the chip?
qa.a: He sensed it was a warning sign but decided he was the problem, because nobody else looked worried.

qa.q: What did Rafiq learn from Irfan's admission that could change how he decides next time?
qa.a: He learned others may hide the same fear, so their calm faces aren't proof something is safe, and his own warning signs count.

qa.q: How might Irfan see the evening now, knowing Rafiq was also scared?
qa.a: Irfan might realise that by hiding his own pain he helped make the dare look easy, and feel a bit responsible.

grounding: A teen goes along with a risky food dare because the group looks comfortable, overriding his own unease.

passage:
Hey Abhinav,
Remember when I laughed at you for spending a whole Sunday visiting PGs? Well. I picked mine in ten minutes, lying on my bed in Aligarh. The listing had 4.8 stars and more than six hundred reviews. Six hundred! I didn't read a single one, didn't ask for a video call, just paid the deposit.
The room is the size of a cupboard. The "daily cleaning" is a boy with a broom on Sundays. Last night I finally scrolled the reviews: half are three words long, posted on the same two days, and my new roommate says the owner gives a free month to anyone who rates him five.
I treated the number like proof. It was just a number.
Next time I'm doing it your way, however boring it is.
Yusuf

qa.q: How many reviews did the PG listing have?
qa.a: It had more than six hundred reviews.

qa.q: What was Yusuf thinking when paying the deposit without reading a single review?
qa.a: Yusuf felt confident, even careless, assuming so many high ratings must mean a good room, so checking seemed unnecessary.

qa.q: What could Yusuf do differently when choosing the next room?
qa.a: Read a few reviews and their dates, ask for a video call or visit, and ask current tenants, the way Abhinav did.

qa.q: How might Abhinav react to this letter, given that Yusuf once laughed at the Sunday of PG visits?
qa.a: Abhinav might feel quietly proven right but also sympathetic, and might offer to help look at the next place.

grounding: A young adult picks a room by its star rating without checking and discovers popularity was not quality.

passage: So, Harish, you asked what happened to my hair. Sit down. I'm Parul, and I trust stars far too much. Before my cousin's engagement, I searched for salons near the women's hostel where I live and picked the one with 4.9 stars and two thousand ratings. Didn't read a thing. Two thousand people, I thought, how bad can it be? I walked in and said, "Just a trim and some layers." The stylist had clearly never done layers. Forty minutes later I looked like a staircase. That night I actually read the reviews. Most were for their other branch across the city, and the recent ones for this branch said "long wait" and "careless." Everyone was rating the name, not the chair I sat in. My cousin was kind about it at the engagement. The photos were not.

qa.q: How many ratings did the salon Parul picked have?
qa.a: It had two thousand ratings and 4.9 stars.

qa.q: Why did Parul feel sure the salon would be fine without reading anything?
qa.a: She thought two thousand people couldn't be wrong, so the huge number felt like proof of quality.

qa.q: What would you advise Parul before she books the next salon?
qa.a: Read the recent reviews for that exact branch, or ask a friend whose haircut she likes, instead of trusting the star count alone.

qa.q: How might Harish see the story as Parul tells it?
qa.a: Harish might find it funny but also recognise the same habit of trusting big numbers in their own choices.

grounding: A young adult chooses a salon by star count without checking and the popularity turns out to mislead.

subtype: Asking whether the crowd knows or just copies [Response]
passage: You asked, Parveen, why your big brother Imran was the only one on our lane not standing in the petrol queue last Tuesday. Okay. At nine that night the lane group lit up: pumps shutting for five days, strike from tomorrow, fill up now. Within an hour the line reached the mosque. Mr Dsouza was there with a jerry can. Even Amjad Bhai, who never panics. I nearly grabbed the keys. Then I asked myself: does anyone in that line actually know, or is everyone just looking at the person in front? Nobody had a source. It was the same forward, over and over. So I rang one person, Sadiq, who drives a tanker for the depot and has no reason to fool me. He laughed. No strike, deliveries normal. I went to bed. Next morning the pump was open, and half the lane was sleepy and grumpy.

qa.q: Who did Imran ring before deciding about the queue?
qa.a: Imran rang Sadiq, who drives a tanker for the depot.

qa.q: How did Imran feel as he watched the line reach the mosque?
qa.a: He felt tempted and uneasy, nearly grabbing the keys, but also doubtful whether anyone in the line actually knew or was just copying the person in front.

qa.q: Which choice turned things for Imran, and why did it work?
qa.a: Ringing Sadiq, one independent person close to the facts, gave him real information instead of the same forward repeated.

qa.q: How might the neighbours who queued half the night see Imran the next morning?
qa.a: They might feel a bit foolish or annoyed that he slept while they waited, and some might ask him first before joining the next rush.

grounding: An adult questions whether the queue knows anything and checks with one independent, trusted source before joining.

subtype: Asking whether the crowd knows or just copies [Response]
passage: I'm Himani, and I sat next to Sarita through our first month at the firm in Pune. By week two, every new joiner in our batch was paying a deposit to the same flat-share agency. Kunal had found it first, then his roommate, then basically all of us. Sarita had the form open on her laptop too. I watched her stop scrolling. She asked the table, "Did any of us actually check this place, or did we all just follow Kunal?" Nobody answered properly. Then she walked over to the relocation desk and talked with Mrs Lobo for a good ten minutes. She came back and quietly closed the form. I don't know exactly what Mrs Lobo told her. Two weeks later, three people from our batch were chasing the agency for their deposits.

qa.q: Where did Sarita go before closing the form?
qa.a: She walked over to the relocation desk and talked with Mrs Lobo.

qa.q: What does Sarita stopping her scrolling and questioning the table suggest she was thinking?
qa.a: She seemed to doubt that the batch had real information and suspected everyone was just following Kunal.

qa.q: What turning point did Sarita choose, and what made it a good one?
qa.a: She went to Mrs Lobo at the relocation desk, a source outside the batch with no stake in the agency, before paying anything.

qa.q: How might the three batchmates chasing their deposits now see Sarita's question at the table?
qa.a: They might wish they had taken it seriously and now see it as sensible caution rather than awkward doubt.

grounding: A colleague watches an adult ask whether the crowd really knows and check one independent source before joining.

subtype: Playground story grows with each telling [Actor]
passage: On Monday, Ingrid told Astrid that the big oak by the school fence in Uppsala had a face in its bark. Astrid, nine, went to look. It was just a knot. On Tuesday, two boys said the face moved its mouth when it rained. On Wednesday, the whole of Class 3 knew that a girl had lost her glove near the roots and never found it, because the oak took it. By Thursday, people ran past it with their hoods up. Astrid did too. On Friday, Ingrid's brother said a teacher had seen it breathe. Astrid had stopped looking at the oak at all. She walked the long way round the football pitch, just in case.

qa.q: What did Astrid find when she first went to look at the bark?
qa.a: It was just a knot.

qa.q: Why did Astrid start walking the long way round, even though she had seen only a knot?
qa.a: Hearing the story from more and more people made it feel truer and scarier, so she avoided the oak just in case.

qa.q: At which point could Astrid have tested the story, and how?
qa.a: Early in the week she could have asked who actually saw the mouth move, or looked at the knot again with a teacher in daylight.

qa.q: How might a teacher feel on hearing children say a teacher had seen the oak breathe?
qa.a: The teacher might be amused but also concerned that the children are frightened, and want to talk about how stories grow.

grounding: A child believes the haunted-tree story more each time more classmates repeat it.

subtype: Playground story grows with each telling [Actor]
passage: Lights-out at the residential school outside Nashik was at nine, and that was when the stories started. The first night, Madhav whispered from the top bunk that the old gulmohar behind Dormitory B dropped flowers only on boys who were going to fail. Darshan, eleven, snorted. The second night, someone in the next row added that a watchman had heard crying in its branches. The third night it was four voices, and the crying had a name. By Saturday, boys carried their buckets the long way to the bathroom block. Darshan told himself it was silly. But when a red flower landed on his shoulder at morning PT, his heart thudded, and he brushed it off before anyone could see.

qa.q: When did the stories start at the school?
qa.a: They started at lights-out, at nine.

qa.q: What does Darshan brushing the flower off before anyone could see suggest?
qa.a: Though he called the story silly, hearing it night after night had made it feel real enough to scare him, and he didn't want others to notice.

qa.q: How could a house parent help after hearing the story grow each night?
qa.a: They could talk calmly with the boys about how a tale grows with each telling, and walk them past the tree in daylight.

qa.q: How might Madhav feel if he learned the story he started now frightened Darshan?
qa.a: Madhav might feel surprised and a little guilty that one whisper grew into something so big.

grounding: A child comes to half-believe a haunted-tree story as it is retold each night by more voices.

passage: The shared jeep from Wadgaon to the high school in the kasba took forty minutes, long enough for a story to grow. On Monday, Francis said he'd heard that Kulkarni Madam kept the library fund for herself. He said "heard" twice. On Tuesday, two girls from Class 9 said she had bought a new scooter with it. On Wednesday nobody said "heard" any more. Samir, fifteen, watched from his corner seat as the story went back and forth like a bag of peanuts. By Friday, students stopped returning library books to her desk and left them with the peon instead. Samir had seen her scooter. It was old and dented. He opened his mouth to say so, then looked at the full jeep and shut it.

qa.q: How long did the shared jeep ride take?
qa.a: It took forty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Samir shut his mouth after opening it to speak?
qa.a: He seemed to feel the whole jeep already treated the story as fact, and was afraid of looking foolish for questioning it.

qa.q: What small step could Samir take after that ride?
qa.a: He could quietly tell Francis what he knew about the old, dented scooter, or ask where the story first came from, starting with one person.

qa.q: What might it be like for Kulkarni Madam when students start leaving books with the peon?
qa.a: She might feel hurt and confused, noticing students avoid her without knowing why, with no way to answer a rumour no one says to her face.

grounding: A student watches a rumour about a teacher harden into accepted fact through repetition.

passage: At the upper school in Aarhus, the story about Mr Holm started as a joke. Valentina, new that term from Madrid, said in chemistry that he handled the burner "like someone who's blown up a lab before." Everyone laughed. The next week, Ulla heard in the cloakroom that he actually had blown up a lab at his old school and been sacked. Then that a student had been hurt. Then a name for the student. Ulla, sixteen, noticed that each version came with more detail and less doubt. Nobody asked Mr Holm. People flinched now when he lit the burner. When Ulla mentioned Valentina's joke, a girl from her class said, "No, it's true, everyone knows." Valentina, sitting nearby, looked uneasy and stayed quiet.

qa.q: What did Valentina first say about Mr Holm?
qa.a: Valentina said he handled the burner "like someone who's blown up a lab before."

qa.q: What might Valentina's uneasy silence reveal about how she felt?
qa.a: Valentina seemed to realise the joke had turned into a "fact" about a real teacher, and may have felt guilty but unsure how to take it back.

qa.q: What could Ulla do, since she knows where the story started?
qa.a: Ulla could calmly tell a trusted teacher, or the class, that it began as a joke, and ask whether anyone actually knows more.

qa.q: How might Mr Holm experience a class that flinches when he lights the burner?
qa.a: He might feel puzzled and uneasy, sensing a distrust he can't explain because nobody has told him the rumour.

grounding: A student observes a joke about a teacher grow into an unquestioned fact with every retelling.

passage:
Dear Mahima,
I owe you an apology, and a letter feels better than a message for this.
On Sunday, when the forward said the dam upstream of Rampur had cracked and everyone should leave before dawn, I sent it to four groups within a minute. I had seen it nine times already. Nine people can't be wrong, I thought. When you replied, "Source? The district office hasn't said anything," I called you heartless in front of the whole family. I said, "If it's true and you did nothing, how will you feel?"
It wasn't true. The photo was of a different dam, from years ago. Nani packed a bag and sat up all night.
You were being careful, not cold. I'm sorry.
Deepak

qa.q: How many times had Deepak seen the dam message before forwarding it?
qa.a: Deepak had seen it nine times already.

qa.q: Why did Deepak call Mahima heartless for asking for a source?
qa.a: Seeing the message so often made it feel certain to Deepak, so doubting it seemed like not caring about people's safety.

qa.q: What could Deepak do the next time a scare message arrives again and again?
qa.a: Pause and check with an official source, like the district office Mahima mentioned, before forwarding it.

qa.q: What was the night like for Nani after the forward reached the family?
qa.a: Nani was frightened enough to pack a bag and sit up all night, a real cost of the false alarm.

grounding: A young adult forwards a scare message because it keeps arriving and treats the one doubter as cold.

passage: Nikita, you asked for a story about something dumb I did in first year. So this is Gautam's confession. During that heatwave, a message went round: "Phones are exploding in pockets above forty-five degrees! Share to save lives!" It came from my class group, my football group, my mother, my mother's friend. By evening I'd seen it about a dozen times, and each time it felt more obviously true. I forwarded it to everyone I knew. My flatmate Tsering just asked, "Is there any actual report?" And I got so annoyed. I told him, "People could get hurt and you want reports?" I made him feel like the villain. A week later, a lecturer showed us the photo was from a battery factory fire abroad. Tsering never said I told you so. I kind of wish he had.

qa.q: Who asked whether there was any actual report?
qa.a: Gautam's flatmate Tsering asked, "Is there any actual report?"

qa.q: What made the message feel more true to Gautam as the evening went on?
qa.a: Seeing it about a dozen times from different people made the repetition feel like proof.

qa.q: At which moment could Gautam have made a different choice?
qa.a: When Tsering asked for a report, Gautam could have paused and looked for one instead of snapping.

qa.q: How might Tsering have felt being treated like the villain for asking one question?
qa.a: Tsering might have felt hurt and unfairly judged, and perhaps less willing to question such messages again.

grounding: A young adult forwards a scare message seen many times and treats the doubting flatmate as careless.

passage: After a news channel showed a leopard attack in a district two hundred kilometres away, Dhanori changed overnight. Preeti watched it happen from the door of her anganwadi near the temple. Parents stopped letting children walk the field path to school, even at noon. Vijay, the sarpanch's son, organised men with sticks to guard the path and had an announcement made on the loudspeaker twice a day. Nobody in Dhanori had seen a leopard in living memory. Meanwhile, every evening, sugarcane tractor-trolleys roared down the main road with no back lights, and boys still rode on top of the loads, waving. Preeti mentioned the trolleys at the panchayat meeting. Vijay nodded politely and went back to the leopard.

qa.q: Who organised men with sticks to guard the path?
qa.a: Vijay, the sarpanch's son, organised them.

qa.q: What might Preeti be worried about when she raises the trolleys at the meeting?
qa.a: She seems worried that the everyday danger of unlit, overloaded trolleys is being ignored while everyone fears a leopard no one has seen.

qa.q: How could Preeti make her point about the trolleys land better?
qa.a: She could describe a concrete near-miss on the main road and suggest one simple step, like back lights, instead of arguing against the leopard fear.

qa.q: Why might Vijay keep returning to the leopard rather than the trolleys?
qa.a: The vivid TV story feels urgent and gives him a visible way to protect people, while the trolleys are familiar and feel normal.

grounding: An adult sees one dramatic news story push the village into over-caution while a common road risk is ignored.

passage: Beatriz had lived on Keurboom Street in Cape Town for two years when the tree story arrived. A storm in another city had dropped an old pine onto a parked car, and the video ran on every news site for days. By the weekend, the residents' association wanted every old tree on the street cut down. Lindiwe from number 14 went door to door with a petition, and people signed fast, still talking about the crushed car. Beatriz signed nothing. She stood at the corner with her coffee and watched the school run: cars speeding down the hill, children dashing across where the pedestrian light had been broken since March. Nobody had petitioned about that. She took a photo of the dead light and wondered who would even look at it.

qa.q: How long had the pedestrian light been broken?
qa.a: It had been broken since March.

qa.q: What was Beatriz feeling as she watched the school run?
qa.a: She seemed uneasy and a bit frustrated that a far-off video had everyone's attention while a daily danger outside was ignored.

qa.q: What could Beatriz do with her photo of the broken light?
qa.a: She could share it with the residents' association and ask Lindiwe to add the crossing to the petition, turning attention to the common risk.

qa.q: How might Lindiwe see the petition differently from Beatriz?
qa.a: Lindiwe probably sees it as protecting neighbours from a real danger shown on the news, not as over-caution.

grounding: An adult watches a vivid story about a rare accident drive the street's caution while an everyday risk goes unfixed.

subtype: Checking source and base rate before spreading [Response]
passage: I'm Tejas, and on Sunday I watched my sister Meher deal with Dadi's water message. It said two hundred people in our city were in hospital from poisoned tap water and nobody should drink it. Dadi had it from three groups and wanted to send it to all her sisters. Meher didn't argue. She sat with the phone and searched the words from the message. Twenty minutes later she found the original: a newspaper report from a different city, three years old. Then she asked Dadi, "In seventy years, how often have you heard of tap water poisoning a whole city here?" Dadi thought. "Never." Meher didn't forward it anywhere. She made Dadi tea and showed her the old article slowly, on the big screen. I can't say what Dadi thought, but she put the phone down.

qa.q: How old was the original report that Meher found?
qa.a: It was three years old, from a different city.

qa.q: What does Dadi putting the phone down suggest she might be feeling?
qa.a: She may have felt reassured, or a little embarrassed, after seeing the old article and realising how rare such an event is.

qa.q: Which part of Meher's approach helped most with Dadi, and why?
qa.a: Asking how often Dadi had heard of this in seventy years let Dadi reach the answer herself, so she didn't feel scolded.

qa.q: How are Dadi's sisters affected by Meher choosing not to forward the message?
qa.a: They are spared a frightening evening of worrying about their drinking water, because the chain stopped with Dadi.

grounding: An adult traces a scare claim to its source, asks how common it is, stops the chain and explains gently to a relative.

subtype: Checking source and base rate before spreading [Response]
passage:
Monday. Leela Masi sent a voice note to the family group at midnight: a gang was stealing kidneys from patients at the city hospital, and everyone should stay away. By morning, Chetan's mother had forwarded it twice.
Wednesday. Chetan, twenty-four, spent his lunch break tracing it. The voice gave no name, no ward, no date. He found the same words in a post from another country, years old. He asked a friend who worked at the hospital how often anything like it had ever been reported there. "Never," she said.
Saturday. At Masi's house, he didn't post a correction in the group. He sat beside her and said, "I know you sent it because you care about us." Then he showed her what he had found. Masi was quiet for a moment, then asked him to help her delete it.

qa.q: Where did Chetan find the same words as the voice note?
qa.a: He found them in a post from another country, years old.

qa.q: Why did Chetan begin by telling Masi he knew she sent it because she cares?
qa.a: He wanted her to feel understood rather than foolish, so she would be open to what he found.

qa.q: What was the turning point in stopping the chain, and why did it work?
qa.a: Chetan chose to talk to Masi in person instead of correcting her in the group, which let her change her mind without losing face.

qa.q: What would change if Chetan had posted a blunt correction in the family group?
qa.a: Leela Masi might have felt embarrassed in front of everyone and defended the message instead of deleting it.

grounding: An adult traces a scare message to its origin, checks how often it happens, and gently stops a relative's forwarding.
